headline: Mission Complete — Trust, But Verify
message:
Monday, 5:27 PM. The engagement log had a final section for Module 3.

--- VALIDATION COMPLETE ---

45.77.180.10 — Development Server:
22/tcp   OpenSSH 7.4 — No critical CVEs requiring validation in this version range.
80/tcp   Apache httpd 2.4.49 — CVE-2021-41773 VALIDATION RESULT:
         PATH TRAVERSAL: CONFIRMED. Safe validation: curl http://45.77.180.10/cgi-bin/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/etc/passwd → HTTP 200, /etc/passwd returned.
         MOD_CGI: INDICATED. curl -I http://45.77.180.10/cgi-bin/ → HTTP 403 (directory configured).
         RCE PREREQUISITE: HIGH LIKELIHOOD — internal configuration verification recommended before exploitation.
         SEVERITY: Path traversal confirmed. RCE prerequisites indicated. Priority: Critical.
443/tcp  Apache httpd 2.4.49 — Same findings apply. Validation deferred to off-peak window — port 443 serves live HTTPS traffic.
3306/tcp [filtered] — Validation not possible. Version and service unknown from external position.

45.77.180.11 — Legacy Server:
22/tcp   OpenSSH 7.4 — No critical CVEs requiring validation.
80/tcp   Apache httpd 2.4.49 — CVE-2021-41773 VALIDATION RESULT:
         PATH TRAVERSAL: INCONCLUSIVE. Safe validation: curl http://45.77.180.11/cgi-bin/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/etc/passwd → HTTP 400 (server rejected traversal URL).
         INDICATOR: Banner shows Apache/2.4.49 (Red Hat). Consistent with RHSA-2021:3610 backport patch.
         STATUS: Possible backport or hardened configuration. Internal review required.
8443/tcp Apache Tomcat 7.0.37 — Validation requires specific CVE selection from the Tomcat 7.0.x CVE list. Deferred to Mission-level planning. End-of-life status documented.

James read through the log. The finding for port 80 on the development server had a different quality from anything they had documented before. Not 'potential match, pending prerequisites.' Not 'version in range, CVSS 9.8.' A specific technique. A specific response. A specific conclusion.

'That feels more real,' he said.

'Because it is more real,' Maya said. 'Everything before this mission was inference. The version number. The CVE. The prerequisites we estimated from our external position. This is the first finding in this engagement that is backed by observed behaviour — a specific request, a specific response, a specific interpretation that matches what the advisory says a vulnerable server does.'

She looked at the inconclusive entry for the legacy server.

'And that one,' James said. 'HTTP 400. Possible backport.'

'Documented correctly,' Maya said. 'Not cleared. Not confirmed. Possible backport, corroborated by the Red Hat suffix. The client's operations team can check the RHSA advisory and confirm whether the patch is applied. If it is, they clear the finding. If it is not, they have a critical finding on the legacy server too.' She paused. 'That is useful information either way. That is what a professional validation report produces.'

James looked at the 443 entry — validation deferred.

'We stopped on port 443.'

'It was 5 PM,' Maya said. 'Port 443 serves the live application layer. I did not want to be the person who confirmed a path traversal finding by accidentally triggering a session error during peak traffic. The client's window for validation testing ends at 5. We documented the deferral and we schedule it tomorrow morning.' She closed the log. 'Professional judgement is knowing when to stop. Not everything that can be tested should be tested right now.'

---

In this mission, you crossed from 'we have potential findings' to 'we have confirmed evidence.'

You learned that validation is its own professional discipline — distinct from assessment and distinct from exploitation. It answers a different question (is the weakness present in this specific environment?) using different techniques (safe, targeted, minimum-necessary probes) and producing a different output (evidence, not just risk estimates).

You learned that patch backports mean the version string is the beginning of the investigation — not the conclusion. A server can display an affected version number while having the vulnerability patched. HTTP 400 on a traversal request, corroborated by a distribution suffix in the banner, is meaningful evidence of a possible backport — and the professionally correct response is documentation of the ambiguity, not a false assurance of safety.

You learned that SAFE — Safe technique, Advisory alignment, Feature confirmed, Evidence documented — is the framework that turns a validation action into a defensible finding. Without SAFE, a validation result is just a note. With SAFE, it is evidence a client can act on, a finding that can survive challenge, and documentation that protects the assessor as much as it informs the client.

You learned when to stop. Validation deferred with a documented reason and a scheduled follow-up is professional. Validation conducted under conditions that risk service disruption or fall outside authorisation is not.

The Meridian Financial engagement now has its first confirmed finding: CVE-2021-41773 path traversal on the development server, with mod_cgi indicated and RCE priority high. The legacy server finding is inconclusive — documented honestly, with the next investigative step identified.

One question remains. Maya asked it as she closed the engagement log.

badgesUnlocked.name: Field Validated
badgesUnlocked.description: Completed Mission 5: Trust, But Verify — applied safe, non-destructive validation techniques to confirm CVE-2021-41773 on the Meridian Financial development server and correctly documented an inconclusive result on the legacy server. Distinguished confirmed findings from false positives, correctly identified the patch backport phenomenon from HTTP 400 responses and distribution banner suffixes, and applied the SAFE framework to produce evidence-based findings.

nextSteps: Module 4: Professional Exploitation Fundamentals — CVE-2021-41773 path traversal is confirmed on the Meridian Financial development server. mod_cgi is indicated. The question Maya asked at the end of this mission — 'Can it actually be exploited safely?' — is what Module 4 answers. Professional exploitation begins with a validated finding and ends with demonstrated, documented impact under controlled conditions.

Optional: Return to the validation lab and repeat the exercise for at least two additional CVEs on different software types. For each one, practise applying SAFE from scratch: compose the validation request manually, interpret the response against the advisory, and document the complete evidence chain.

Review: The five-mission framework is now complete. PING (host discovery) → OCF (port states) → BVR (service identity) → CPR (CVE research) → SAFE (validation). Each mission built the input for the next. Every finding in Module 3 is now documented, evidence-based, and ready for controlled exploitation.
